Next movement for continuity and structure:
-- Jonah introduces Adrian as he enters with two more people; they all greet Mara together, then continue the conversation from before she arrived.
-- Mara joins the group and contributes to their ongoing conversation about how nonverbal cue-reading relates to other forms of human connection.
-- The five adults play the calibration frame game. Mara participates, but her uncertainty increases as her nonverbal behavior is read correctly in ways she doesn't understand; she can't guess who will win.
-- Adrian names and thanks the reader, then announces he must go; this is not a social farewell to them. They watch him walk out and return to talking about cue-reading until the game interrupts again.
-- Mara keeps track of time, noting when the adult newcomer should have entered but hasn't yet, and when it becomes a little later than she thought it would.

Manuscript
The next moment, two people approached from behind the catering worker—the leader of this week’s Fulcrum group, she guessed. He was middle-aged, with brown hair combed forward over a partially balding head and dark-framed glasses on a nose that looked like it had been broken at least once in his life. He was tall, well-muscled, and holding two glass wine bottles in his hand. And he walked up to the low table in the corner, greeted his four group members, and asked for help uncorking some of the new arrivals’ wine.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

And that was when a door opened down the hallway behind her, releasing two voices into the room. One female, one male; one asking a question, the other replying; neither loud nor excited, just casual conversation. Jonah released her hand and turned away to look down the hall at them.
When Mara heard the voices and followed his gaze, she saw one young man who wasn’t Jonah, but close in size and shape; he had brown hair and a beard and was carrying a glass.

The brown-haired man glanced once over his shoulder, saw them standing there, nodded hello, and stepped right into the gathering, holding up his glass of wine—a half-full plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo on it. “Cheers.” He set it on the table against the wall to the left of the door, and stepped forward to shake Jonah’s hand as they exchanged names.

As he set down the glass and moved out of its space, a previously unseen catering worker entered from the hallway behind him and retrieved it. She wore the same black-and-white striped Fulcrum uniform shirt, though she looked old enough to have had that job since the Institute was founded; and she gave no outward sign of the social fact that she was taking their discarded drink back to the kitchen, while the rest of the conversation went on.

Mara watched this woman return to the hallway where she belonged, and noticed herself noticing who assumed whose labor.

segment:
Adrian is here, but he didn’t want to interrupt or embarrass her just now, so he waited in the hallway as he approached and then took his time walking in. She heard his footsteps but was watching Jonah when Adrian spoke, so she spun to look. He stood near her with the same calm self-control of a man in his thirties who expects everyone’s attention.
“Jonah, good to see you again,” he said, shaking that same hand she’d just been holding.
Jonah grinned back at him, but for Mara it felt as though his gaze skimmed her without settling or touching. She was beginning to feel that she might be a wall. She needed to open up, let him get to know her—
“And I hope you’re doing well today, Mara?” Adrian had turned to her, one arm extended in greeting.
Mara smiled at him, trying not to let him see the flicker of surprise at his use of her name.

“Thank you,” she replied. “Yes, I am.” She watched as he extended his hand to her; when she took it, he shook it gently, fingers only lightly clenched and one other hand just resting on the wrist, in a gesture that spoke of politeness without any pressure to be pleased.
As they released each other, she realized she didn’t know what to do next, now that her cue was over.

Adrian held her gaze and waited without pressure or obligation.
In fact, he seemed genuinely interested in her choice; even his expression held the subtle inflection of wondering.
She opened her mouth to answer but found only the question “What do you want me to do?”

segment:
And then there was another person coming down the hallway, also dressed in a black-and-white striped uniform, walking purposefully toward them without looking at them; until, glancing up in Mara’s direction, he paused—took an instant to process something she saw him notice in his periphery.
That pause gave Mara time to focus on this newcomer, who wore a white baseball cap with the Fulcrum logo over his neat brown hair, and turned out to be Adrian. He looked around for a seat, saw the couch where Jonah had been sitting, and sat there—while Mara and Jonah made the introductions they would have made if he hadn’t interrupted.

They still were, she realized, waiting to see what he would say.
When he looked up at her, she saw it in his eyes first; the same faint flicker of curiosity she’d noticed when he’d stopped in the hallway, before he knew who was here. Then, looking down at the glass on the table next to him, he said, “Did you notice?”

“Yes.”
“Me, too. Tell me what you saw.”
Mara waited, still uncertain.
Adrian grinned. “Just tell me what you noticed. I want to hear how you frame it.”

She hesitated another second.
He prompted her again with his eyes—and then she knew that she was going to have to say it out loud. “I just noticed how she saw that we weren’t finished with that drink. How he gave it to her, without any words. It seemed…” Mara paused again, not wanting to say what it seemed like.

“Well,” said Adrian, “I noticed the same thing.”
